subject: Cognitive Science
title: Exemplar Theory
description: A micro-lesson that makes Exemplar Theory usable.

hook.text: Maybe you don't store one ideal bird. Maybe you store every bird you've ever encountered.

buildup.text: Exemplar theory says categories are collections of remembered instances, not abstractions.

discovery.text: You classify a new animal by comparing it to specific dogs, cats, and birds you've actually seen.

twist.text: This explains why personal experience warps categories. A vet's "typical dog" differs from yours.

climax.text: Exemplar models beat prototypes at capturing unusual or highly variable categories.

quiz.question: How does exemplar theory differ from prototype theory?
options: It stores specific instances instead of an ideal summary

details.summary: Exemplar theory proposes that categories are represented not by a single prototype but by stored memories of specific encountered examples. When classifying a new item, the brain compares it to all remembered instances. This explains why we can handle highly variable categories and unusual members.
details.whyItMatters: Exemplar theory explains how people categorize despite enormous within-category variation. It accounts for context effects that prototype theory cannot easily handle.
takeaways: Categories are stored as collections of individual examples
Classification involves comparing to remembered instances
Exemplar models handle high variability better than prototypes

faq.question: How does exemplar theory differ from prototype theory?
faq.answer: Prototype theory stores one summary representation per category. Exemplar theory stores every encountered instance. When classifying, prototype theory compares to the average; exemplar theory compares to all stored examples. Exemplar theory preserves information about variability and exceptions.

faq.question: Which theory is correct, exemplar or prototype?
faq.answer: Both capture real aspects of categorization. People likely use prototypes for well-known categories and exemplars for smaller or more variable ones. Hybrid models that combine both approaches often fit behavioral data better than either alone.
